name: Judeo-Arabic of Fez, 'le parler arabe des Juifs de Fès'
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Brunot, Louis. 1936. Notes sur le parler arabe des Juifs de Fès. Hespéris 22 (fasc. 1): 1-32.
catalog_quote: Le parler judéo-arabe se distingue par un accent très particulier qu'il est difficile de définir. Est-ce un accent tonique, est-ce le timbre, est-ce un accent de phrase ? On ne saurait le dire. En tout cas, il est certain que les syllabes ne sont pas accentuées d'après leur place dans le mot, mais d'après leur place dans la phrase ou le membre de phrase. Par surcroît, tout comme en français, le sentiment du sujet parlant lui laisse la liberté d'accentuer, selon son état affectif, tantôt une syllabe, tantôt l'autre dans le même mot, dans une même phrase.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.translation: The Judeo-Arabic dialect is distinguished by a very peculiar accent that is hard to define. Is it a tonic accent, is it timbre, is it a phrase accent? One cannot say. In any case, it is certain that syllables are not accented according to their place in the word, but according to their place in the phrase or phrase-member. Moreover, just as in French, the speaker's feeling leaves him free to accent, according to his affective state, now one syllable, now another in the same word, in the same phrase.

new_statements.rule_in_words: No word-level stress rule: prominence is assigned by position in the phrase (or phrase-member), not by position in the word, and may shift with the speaker's affect; the author cannot decide whether it is stress, timbre or phrasal accent.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the author notes speaker-dependent, affect-driven variation within the same word and phrase.
new_statements.domain_note: Explicitly phrase-level; the dialect described is the Jewish Arabic of Fez (data gathered with Elie Malka). No citation-form statement.
new_statements.identity_note: Brunot 1936 describes the Judeo-Arabic of Fez (Fès) specifically, one Jewish Moroccan dialect within jude1265 (no separate glottocode). Glottolog's reference list for jude1265 also includes Constantine (Algeria: Tirosh-Becker) and Sousse (Tunisia: Saada) items that are not Moroccan; none of those were used. Heath 2002 (the scan's named source) covers ~30 Jewish dialects and remains unopened.

sources.note: Section IV 'Accent', §24 (p. 15): the Jewish dialect has a peculiar accent hard to define (tonic? timbre? phrasal?); syllables are certainly NOT stressed according to their position in the word but according to their position in the phrase or phrase-member, and the speaker may shift it for affective reasons.
